title: State complexity of complementing unambiguous automata
formal: For each integer \(n\geq1\), define \[C(n)=\max_{A}\ \min\{\lvert Q_B\rvert: L(B)=\{0,1\}^{*}\setminus L(A)\},\] where \(A\) ranges over all unambiguous finite automata with between 1 and \(n\) states over the binary alphabet, and \(B\) ranges over nondeterministic finite automata over that alphabet with at least one state. Determine the asymptotic growth of \(C(n)\) up to multiplicative constant factors. The output automaton is allowed to be ambiguous.
why: Unambiguity limits the number of positive certificates without directly describing negative certificates. The optimal cost of complementing this representation measures how much succinctness is lost under logical negation and tests the reach of communication-based lower bounds for finite-state models.
status_note: Primary 2022 papers and the 2025 unary-language paper describe a gap between quasipolynomial lower and exponential upper bounds for binary alphabets. A bounded search on 13 September 2026 found no matching general bound. Source claims and preprint statements have not been independently proof-verified.

progress.text: Raskin proves a superpolynomial lower bound using unary automata.
The revised binary construction gives the stronger lower bound \(n^{\widetilde{\Omega}(\log n)}\).
The revised upper-bound paper proves \(\sqrt{n+1}\,2^{n/2}\) states suffice for every input UFA.
The updated unary-language paper gives quasipolynomial unary complementation; it was subsequently published in 2025. This does not close the binary gap.

sentences: An unambiguous finite automaton has at most one accepting run for each word.
For a binary alphabet, this card asks for the worst-case number of states in a smallest nondeterministic automaton accepting its complement.
The input has at most n states, while the output may be ambiguous and may have multiple initial states.
Known binary lower bounds are quasipolynomial and known general upper bounds are exponential; stronger unary results concern a different alphabet.
The requested answer gives matching multiplicative constant-factor bounds on the state count, proved in Lean.

context_blocks.text: Section 5.11 asks for better bounds on the number of states needed to complement unambiguous automata, emphasizing the gap for binary and larger alphabets. This benchmark makes the binary-alphabet extremal state count the single target and asks for matching multiplicative bounds.

The consolidated 2018 source also asks whether general-alphabet complementation can require an exponential number of states. That endpoint motivates the gap but is not equivalent to determining the entire asymptotic rate.

Göös, Kiefer and Yuan prove a binary-alphabet lower bound \(n^{\widetilde{\Omega}(\log n)}\) even when the complement may be represented ambiguously. Here the tilde suppresses powers of \(\log\log n\) in the exponent.

Indzhev and Kiefer give a complement with at most \(\sqrt{n+1}\,2^{n/2}\) states even with an unambiguous output. Their matching analysis of that specific conversion does not prove an exponential lower bound on the smallest possible complement.
The later unary-alphabet result gives quasipolynomial complementation there and still distinguishes the much wider binary-alphabet gap.

source_consolidations.note: The source asks whether complementing unambiguous automata over general alphabets can require exponential size. This is a proposed hard endpoint of the complementation gap, not an equivalent restatement of every weaker improvement target.

definitions: Both kinds of automaton are finite tuples \((Q,\{0,1\},\Delta,I,F)\), where \(Q\) is the state set, \(I,F\subseteq Q\) are the initial and final state sets, and \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\{0,1\}\times Q\) is a transition relation. Multiple initial states, missing transitions, unreachable states and empty initial or final sets are allowed. There are no epsilon transitions or duplicate parallel transitions.

An accepting run on a word \(a_1\cdots a_m\) is a state sequence \(q_0,\ldots,q_m\) with \(q_0\in I\), \(q_m\in F\), and \((q_{i-1},a_i,q_i)\in\Delta\) for every \(1\leq i\leq m\). A word belongs to the language if it has an accepting run. For the empty word the accepting runs are the states in \(I\cap F\). The input automaton is unambiguous when each word has at most one accepting run; there is no restriction on the number of rejecting runs.

Only the number of states is charged, not transitions, the alphabet description or computation used to construct the automaton. Up to state renaming there are finitely many eligible inputs. Determinization and complementation give an output with at most \(2^{n}\) states, so the minimum and maximum defining \(C(n)\) exist.

The target is a positive real-valued comparison function \(g\) on the positive integers, together with constants \(c_1,c_2>0\) and an integer \(n_0\geq1\), such that \(c_1g(n)\leq C(n)\leq c_2g(n)\) for every \(n\geq n_0\). Matching only the order of \(\log C(n)\) is weaker than this criterion. The function must specify an asymptotic rate rather than restate the defining automaton optimization.
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of matching upper and lower bounds within constant factors for \(C(n)\) as defined. The upper bound must cover every eligible input automaton; the lower bound must give a worst-case input for every sufficiently large size bound. No efficiency requirement is imposed on the conversion algorithm. Bounds only for one particular conversion, unary inputs, or unambiguous outputs do not supply the required matching result.
